    SimCLR

    Pseudocode

    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  x_i, x_j = augment(x), augment(x)
  h_i, h_j = f(x_i), f(x_j)  # shared
  z_i, z_j = g(h_i), g(h_j)
  z = normalize(cat([z_i, z_j]))  # 2N
  sim = z @ z.T
  sim.fill_diagonal_(-inf)  # self
  pos = (arange(2N) + N) % 2N
  loss = cross_entropy(sim / tau, pos)
  loss.backward(); opt.step()  # both
# after training: keep f, use h
del g  # head discarded
h = f(x)  # 2,048-d features

    MoCo and MoCo v2

    Pseudocode

    for x in loader:
  x_q, x_k = aug(x), aug(x)
  # f_k initialized from f_q
  q = f_q(x_q)  # N x C
  k = f_k(x_k).detach()
  # queue: C x K keys, past batches
  l_pos = (q * k).sum(1, True)  # N x 1
  l_neg = q @ queue  # N x K
  logits = cat([l_pos, l_neg], 1)
  labels = zeros(N)  # positive at 0
  loss = CE(logits / t, labels)
  loss.backward(); opt.step()  # f_q
  f_k = m * f_k + (1 - m) * f_q
  enqueue(queue, k); dequeue(queue)
# v2: MLP head, blur, cosine lr, t=0.2

    Query and key views

    • crop, color jitter, flip, grayscale (v1)
    • Two random views of one patch; training pulls them together.

    Two encoders

    • query encoder, trained by backpropagation
    • key encoder: no gradients, initialized from f_q
    • The key encoder is a slow, gradient-free copy of the query encoder.

    Normalized embeddings

    • 128 ResNet-50, then fc to 128-d, ℓ2-normalized
    • detached; key batch shuffled across GPUs (shuffling BN)
    • Each view becomes a unit vector: or .

    Dictionary as a queue

    • negatives come from the queue, decoupled from the batch size (256)
    • The dictionary of negatives can be far bigger than the batch.

    InfoNCE over keys

    • the key of the same image, at index 0
    • 0.07 in v1
    • Train to find its own key among .

    EMA update

    • momentum, 0.999
    • Slow drift keeps old and new keys in the queue comparable.

    Update the queue

    • queue keys from recent batches by a slowly changing encoder
    • This batch’s keys join; the oldest batch leaves.

    MoCo intuition

    Why a large number of negatives helps

    Many negatives push the model to learn more discriminative, more generalizable representations.

    Imagine training with only 2 negatives

    A pathology foundation model trained with contrastive learning. The query is an H&E patch with tumor cells.

    • Positive another augmented view of the same patch
    • Negative 1 an adipose tissue patch
    • Negative 2 a background tissue patch

    These negatives are easy to tell apart from the query. The model can get by with simple features, without understanding subtler histological differences.

    Now imagine 65,536 negatives

    The queue holds embeddings from many different tissue patches:

    • adipose tissue
    • normal epithelium
    • tumor cells
    • inflammatory cells
    • different tumor morphologies

    Now the model meets hard negatives: patches that look like the query but come from different images, such as two tumor patches with very similar nuclear morphology.

    To tell them apart, the model must learn more detailed features. That is what makes the representation more discriminative.

    More negatives → more hard negatives → finer, more discriminative features

    MoCo v3

    Pseudocode

    for x in loader:
  x1, x2 = aug(x), aug(x)
  # f_k: f_q copy, no pred head
  q1, q2 = f_q(x1), f_q(x2)
  k1, k2 = f_k(x1), f_k(x2)
  loss = ctr(q1,k2) + ctr(q2,k1)
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  f_k = m*f_k + (1-m)*f_q
def ctr(q, k):
  logits = q @ k.T  # N x N
  labels = arange(N)  # diag
  ce = CE(logits / t, labels)
  return 2 * t * ce
# inside the ViT, random init:
tok = stop_grad(patch_proj(x))
# downstream: keep f_q backbone

    Two views

    • random crop, color jitter, blur, solarize, flip, grayscale
    • Two random views of one patch; each goes through both encoders.

    Two encoders

    • query encoder, trained by backpropagation
    • key encoder, an EMA of f_q: no gradients, no prediction head
    • The extra prediction head on the query side breaks the symmetry, as in BYOL.

    Normalized embeddings

    • 256 output size of both heads, ℓ2-normalized
    • detached: keys carry no gradient
    • Both views go through both encoders, giving two queries and two keys.

    Keys from the same batch

    • batch size, 4096; the other N − 1 keys are negatives
    • labels the positive of row i is column i
    • No queue: a large batch already holds thousands of negatives.

    Symmetrized InfoNCE

    • temperature, 0.2
    • a constant scale on the loss
    • Each query must pick out its own key among the keys, in both directions.

    EMA update

    • momentum, 0.99
    • A slowly moving key encoder gives stable targets.

    Stable ViT training

    • first layer: linear projection of 16 × 16 patches to tokens
    • dips sudden accuracy drops, caused by gradient spikes
    • Freezing the first layer at its random init removes most dips and adds accuracy.

    BackboneResNet-50ViT (ResNet also works)

    LossOne directionSymmetrized over both views
    Patch projectionNot applicableRandom init, frozen

    BYOL

    Pseudocode

    for x in loader:
  v1, v2 = aug(x), aug(x)
  # tg: EMA of online, no pred
  p1, p2 = q(on(v1)), q(on(v2))
  z1, z2 = tg(v1), tg(v2)
  loss = mse(p1,z2) + mse(p2,z1)
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  tg = tau*tg + (1-tau)*on
def mse(p, z):  # no negatives
  p, z = norm(p), norm(z)
  return 2 - 2*(p*z).sum(-1)
# no collapse: predictor q
# + stop-grad + EMA target
# downstream: keep encoder f

    Two views

    • two augmentation pipelines: crop, color jitter, flip, grayscale, blur, solarize
    • Two random views of one patch; each takes a turn as the online input.

    Online and target networks

    • online weights, trained by backpropagation
    • target weights: an EMA of θ, no gradient
    • Only the online side has the predictor, which makes the two branches asymmetric.

    Prediction and target

    • 256 output size of the projector and the predictor
    • target output, behind a stop-gradient
    • The online network predicts the target’s projection of the other view.

    Normalized MSE

    • ℓ2-normalized prediction and target
    • negatives none: the loss only pulls pairs together
    • Make the prediction point the same way as the target.

    Symmetrized loss

    • the same loss with the two views swapped
    • gradient flows into θ only; the target is behind a stop-gradient
    • Both views take a turn as the input to the online network.

    EMA update

    • momentum, 0.996 rising to 1
    • A slowly moving target gives stable regression targets.

    Why it does not collapse

    • collapse the same output for every image: zero loss, useless features
    • no predictor the representation collapses
    • target copies the online network each step: training fails
    • With no negatives, the asymmetry between the two branches keeps the features from collapsing.

    BYOL vs contrastive methods

    ComponentSimCLR, MoCoBYOL
    NegativesRequired: batch or queueNone
    Second branchSame network (SimCLR) or EMA keys (MoCo)EMA target network
    HeadsProjection MLPProjection + predictor, online side only
    LossInfoNCENormalized MSE: 2 − 2 cos
    Avoids collapse byPushing negatives apartPredictor, stop-gradient and EMA
    • ImageNet linear probe: ResNet-50 74.3%.

    Barlow Twins

    Pseudocode

    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  y_a, y_b = augment(x), augment(x)
  h_a, h_b = f(y_a), f(y_b)  # shared
  z_a, z_b = g(h_a), g(h_b)  # N x D
  z_a = (z_a - z_a.mean(0)) / z_a.std(0)
  z_b = (z_b - z_b.mean(0)) / z_b.std(0)
  c = z_a.T @ z_b / N  # D x D
  on = ((diag(c) - 1) ** 2).sum()
  off = (off_diagonal(c) ** 2).sum()
  loss = on + lambd * off
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
# after training: keep f, use h

    Two augmented views

    • crop, flip, color jitter, grayscale, blur, solarization

    A wide projector

    • projector: 3 linear layers of 8,192 units
    • BN, ReLU after the first two layers

    Standardize each dimension over the batch

    • mean and standard deviation of dimension over the batch
    • a sample in the batch (2,048 in the paper)

    Cross-correlation between the views

    • , entries between −1 and 1
    • embedding dimensions, not samples

    Barlow Twins loss

    • 5 × 10⁻³, weights the redundancy term
    • invariance: each dimension agrees across views
    • redundancy reduction: dimensions decorrelate

    Target

    • identity matrix
    • no negatives, predictor, stop-gradient or EMA teacher

    VICReg

    Pseudocode

    for x in loader:
  x_a, x_b = augment(x), augment(x)
  y_a, y_b = f(x_a), f(x_b)
  z_a, z_b = h(y_a), h(y_b)  # N x D
  sim = mse_loss(z_a, z_b); v = c = 0
  for z in (z_a, z_b):  # each branch
    std = sqrt(z.var(0) + 1e-4)
    v += relu(1 - std).mean()
  for z in (z_a, z_b):
    C = cov(z)  # D x D
    c += off_diag(C).pow(2).sum() / D
  loss = 25 * sim + 25 * v + 1 * c
  loss.backward(); opt.step()

    Two augmented views

    • the image; and are its two views
    • crop, flip, color jitter, grayscale, blur, solarization

    An encoder per branch

    • encoder (ResNet-50); its 2,048-d output is kept
    • usually equal to , but the branches may differ

    Expander

    • expander: 3 layers of 8,192 units, discarded after training
    • a batch of embeddings, not normalized

    Invariance

    • batch size (2,048 in the paper)
    • the only term that links the two branches
    • Invariance: Pulls two augmented views of the same image closer together.

    Variance (hinge on the std)

    • target standard deviation, 1
    • 10⁻⁴, keeps the square root stable
    • dimension across the batch, per branch
    • Variance: Prevents different images from all being mapped to the same representation.

    Covariance, within each branch

    • covariance within one branch
    • vs. Barlow Barlow Twins correlates the two branches
    • Covariance: Encourages different embedding dimensions to carry nonredundant information.

    Total loss

    • ImageNet defaults
    • no negatives, stop-gradient, predictor or normalization
    • Invariance: Pulls two augmented views of the same image closer together.
    • Variance: Prevents different images from all being mapped to the same representation.
    • Covariance: Encourages different embedding dimensions to carry nonredundant information.

    DINO

    Pseudocode

    # x: unlabeled H&E patch
for x in wsi_patches:
  crops = multi_crop(x)
  v_s = crops  # 2 global + n local
  v_t = crops[:2]  # same globals
  s = student(v_s)
  # teacher: stop gradient
  with no_grad():
    t = teacher(v_t)
  p_s = softmax(s / tau_s)
  # center, then sharpen
  p_t = softmax((t - c) / tau_t)
  # teacher global i vs student view j
  loss = mean(H(p_t[i], p_s[j])
    for i in (0, 1)
    for j in views if j != i)
  loss.backward()
  optimizer.step()  # student
  teacher = ema(teacher, student)
  c = ema(c, t.mean(0))

    Pseudocode

    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  z = dvae(x)  # 196 ids, frozen
  p = patchify(x)  # 196 x 768
  m = block_mask(0.4)
  p[m] = e_M  # learnable [M]
  h = encoder(p + pos)
  logits = head(h[m])  # 8192
  loss = CE(logits, z[m])
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
# after: drop head, fine-tune
# v2: CLIP-distilled tokenizer

    Two views of one image

    • the DALL-E dVAE, trained separately, frozen
    • visual words in the codebook
    • Each patch gets a discrete “word”: the answer key.

    Blockwise masking

    • blocks of 16+ patches, about 40% in total
    • one learnable mask embedding
    • Whole blocks can’t be filled in from neighbours.

    Encoder sees every position

    • ViT-B/16 or ViT-L/16
    • vs. MAE [M] tokens are encoded too: more compute
    • Visible patches and [M] tokens are encoded together.

    Predict the visual token

    • linear layer to 8,192 classes
    • At each masked position, classify which visual word belongs there.

    Masked image modeling loss

    • only masked positions contribute
    • BERT for images: the “words” are visual tokens.

    After pretraining

    • 83.2% ViT-B after fine-tuning on ImageNet-1K
    • 56.7% ViT-B linear probe: frozen features are weak
    • Use BEiT as an initialization to fine-tune, not as a frozen feature extractor.

    MAE

    Pseudocode

    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  p = patchify(x)  # B x 196 x 768
  keep, mask = random_masking(0.75)
  z = encoder(p[keep] + pos[keep])
  t = cat([z, m.repeat(n_masked)])
  t = unshuffle(t) + pos
  p_hat = decoder(t)
  # p_hat: pixels for all 196 patches
  y = (p - p.mean(-1)) / p.std(-1)
  err = ((p_hat - y) ** 2).mean(-1)
  loss = err[mask].mean()
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
# after: keep encoder, drop decoder

    Patchify

    • one 16 × 16 px patch (7 × 7 of 196 shown)

    Random masking

    • masked patches, sampled uniformly at random

    Encoder on visible patches only

    • ViT encoder (ViT-B/16, L/16, H/14)
    • positional embedding of patch
    • 25% of tokens enter the encoder, so pretraining is cheaper

    Mask tokens join the sequence

    • one shared, learned mask token

    Lightweight decoder

    • decoder: 8 blocks, 512-d, about 9% of ViT-L’s FLOPs per token

    Reconstructed pixels

    • 768 = 16 × 16 × 3 pixel values per patch

    Loss on masked patches

    • mean and std of patch i’s own pixels
    • the loss is computed on masked patches only

    Downstream

    • discarded after pretraining
    • aug. random crop and flip only

    iBOT

    Pseudocode

    # x: unlabeled H&E patch
for x in wsi_patches:
  crops = multi_crop(x)
  m = block_masks(crops[:2])
  v_t = crops[:2]  # unmasked
  f_cls, f_tok = backbone(crops, m)
  s_cls = head(f_cls)  # shared
  s_tok = head(f_tok[m])
  with no_grad():  # teacher
    t_cls, t_tok = teacher(v_t)
  p_s = softmax(s_cls / tau_s)
  q_s = softmax(s_tok / tau_s)
  p_t = softmax((t_cls - c) / tau_t)
  q_t = softmax((t_tok[m] - c2) / tau_t2)
  l_cls = H(p_t, p_s)  # other view
  l_mim = H(q_t, q_s)  # same view
  loss = l_cls + l_mim
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  teacher = ema(teacher, student)
  c, c2 = ema(c, t_cls), ema(c2, t_tok)

    Pseudocode

    # x: unlabeled H&E patch
for x in wsi_patches:
  crops = multi_crop(x)
  m = random_masks(crops[:2])
  v_t = crops[:2]  # unmasked
  f_cls, f_tok = backbone(crops, m)
  s_cls = dino_head(f_cls)
  s_tok = ibot_head(f_tok[m])
  with no_grad():  # teacher
    t_cls, t_tok = teacher(v_t)
  p_s = softmax(s_cls / tau_s)
  q_s = softmax(s_tok / tau_s)
  p_t = sinkhorn(t_cls / tau_t)
  q_t = sinkhorn(t_tok[m] / tau_t)
  l_dino = H(p_t, p_s)  # other views
  l_ibot = H(q_t, q_s)  # same crop
  l_koleo = koleo(f_cls)  # per view
  loss = l_dino + l_ibot + 0.1 * l_koleo
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  teacher = ema(teacher, student)

    CLIP

    Pseudocode

    # N (image, caption) pairs from the web
for imgs, texts in loader:
  i_e = l2norm(image_enc(imgs) @ W_i)
  t_e = l2norm(text_enc(texts) @ W_t)
  # both: N x d_e, unit length
  logits = exp(t) * i_e @ t_e.T  # N x N
  labels = arange(N)  # diagonal
  loss = (CE(logits, labels)
        + CE(logits.T, labels)) / 2
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  t.clamp_(max=log(100))
# zero-shot, no training
T = l2norm(text_enc(prompts) @ W_t)
pred = argmax(i_e @ T.T)

    A batch of image–caption pairs

    • pairs per batch (32,768 in the paper)
    • the web text that came with image ; ~400M pairs in total

    Image embedding

    • image encoder: ResNet or ViT
    • a linear projection only, no MLP head
    • random square crop is the only augmentation

    Text embedding

    • text Transformer; the [EOS] token is the feature
    • a linear projection only

    One shared space

    • the joint dimension (512 for ViT-B/32)
    • so a dot product is a cosine

    similarity logits

    • image scored against caption
    • a learned log-scale

    Symmetric cross-entropy

    • rows: each image picks its caption
    • columns: each caption picks its image

    What training does

    • mismatched pairs act as negatives
    • gap images and captions keep separate regions

    Learned temperature

    • softmax temperature, learned as
    • 100 cap that keeps training stable

    Zero-shot classification

    • embedding of “an H&E image of {label}.”
    • any class you can name; no retraining

    CoCa

    Pseudocode

    # x: images, y: caption token ids
for x, y in loader:
  v = vit(x)  # B x 256 x D
  v_gen = gen_pool(v)  # 256 q
  e_x = con_pool(v_gen)  # 1 q
  h = uni_dec(cat([y, cls]))
  e_y = h[:, -1]  # [CLS]
  l_con = clip_loss(e_x, e_y, sigma)
  z = multi_dec(h[:, :-1], v_gen)
  # next-token prediction
  l_cap = CE(z[:, :-1], y[:, 1:])
  loss = 1.0 * l_con + 2.0 * l_cap
  loss.backward()  # one pass, both
# embeddings: zero-shot, retrieval
# decoder: captions, VQA

    An image–caption pair

    • the image (288 × 288 in pretraining)
    • alt-text, or JFT label names in a prompt

    Image tokens

    • ViT 18 × 18 patches, so 16 × 16 = 256 tokens
    • width; encoder 86M (Base) to 1B (CoCa)

    Attentional pooler

    • generative pooler: 256 queries, fed to the decoder
    • contrastive pooler: 1 query, on top of the first

    Unimodal text decoder

    • learnable token appended to the caption
    • causal token sees only tokens up to ; no image

    Contrastive loss

    • normalized image and [CLS] embeddings
    • learnable temperature, starting at 0.07

    Multimodal text decoder

    • split decoder layers cut in half: 12 + 12 (Base, Large)
    • cross-attn text queries; image keys and values

    Captioning loss

    • the true earlier tokens (teacher forcing)
    • softmax over the vocabulary at step

    One objective

    • λ_Con = 1, λ_Cap = 2 in the paper
    • cost 1.18× contrastive-only; one forward–backward

    Two ways to use it

    • zero-shot classification and retrieval
    • captioning and question answering

    I-JEPA

    Pseudocode

    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  blocks = sample_targets(4)  # 15-20%
  ctx = sample_context()  # 85-100%
  ctx = ctx - union(blocks)
  s_x = ctx_enc(x, keep=ctx)
  with no_grad():
    s_y = tgt_enc(x)  # full image
  loss = 0
  for b in blocks:
    queries = mask_token + pos_embed[b]
    pred = predictor(s_x, queries)
    loss += l2(pred, s_y[b])
  loss = loss / len(blocks)
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  tgt_enc = ema(tgt_enc, ctx_enc)

    Target blocks

    • patch indices of target block ; blocks may overlap
    • size 15–20% of the image each, aspect ratio 0.75–1.5

    Context block

    • one block covering 85–100% of the image, square
    • patches inside any target block are removed

    Context encoder

    • context encoder (ViT), sees only the context patches

    Target encoder, masked after encoding

    • target encoder, sees the full image
    • targets are masked after encoding, not before

    Predictor, once per block

    • narrow ViT predictor (384-d), run once per block
    • shared mask token plus the position of target patch

    Loss in representation space

    • distance in representation space, not pixels

    EMA target encoder

    • momentum, 0.996 rising linearly to 1
    • used downstream, average-pooled; no [CLS] token

    DINOv2 for pathology

    Pseudocode

    # DINOv2 loop; two swaps for tissue
for tiles in loader:

    DINOv3 intuition

    How Gram anchoring works, step by step

    The Gram matrix keeps only how patches relate to each other. Anchoring it to a clean teacher keeps dense features sharp during very long training.

    Patch features

    The backbone gives one token per patch. Stack the patch tokens of a global crop as the rows of . Here and . In DINOv3 a 256 px crop gives and .

    L2-normalize each row

    Divide every row by its length, so each patch vector has unit norm. Dot products between rows are now cosine similarities.

    Build the Gram matrix

    Multiply by its transpose. Entry is the similarity of patches and , and the diagonal is 1. It records which patches look alike, and nothing else.

    The Gram teacher’s matrix

    The same matrix from the Gram teacher: an earlier EMA snapshot whose patch features were still clean, fed a image and then downsampled. Same-tissue patches are similar, different tissues are not. The student’s patches have drifted toward one shared direction, so everything looks alike.

    Compare the two

    Subtract them and square every entry. The Gram loss is the sum: the squared Frobenius norm of .

    Anchor the student

    Gradients flow only into the student. Each step nudges its patch features until their pairwise similarities match the teacher’s. Rotating all rows by the same leaves unchanged, so DINO and iBOT stay free to improve the features themselves.

    Gram anchoring constrains patch similarities, not the features themselves.

    DINOv2 intuition

    How KoLeo works, step by step

    KoLeo spreads the class tokens of a batch evenly over the sphere, so features stay diverse and nearest-neighbour search works well.

    Tokens on the sphere

    Take the class tokens of the images in a small batch and ℓ2-normalize them, so every sits on the unit sphere. Real tokens have hundreds of dimensions; the circle is a 2D picture.

    Nearest neighbour

    For each token, find the closest other token in the batch. Only this one distance enters the loss; every other token is ignored.

    Log penalty

    Take minus the log of that distance. A far neighbour costs little, a close one costs a lot, and the cost has no upper limit as .

    Average: KoLeo loss

    Average the penalties over the batch. This is the Kozachenko–Leonenko estimate of differential entropy, up to scale and constants, so lowering the loss raises the entropy of the features. DINOv2 adds it with weight 0.1.

    Push apart

    The gradient pushes each token straight away from its nearest neighbour , harder the closer they are. Repeated over training, the batch spreads evenly over the sphere.

    Near-duplicates

    Even spread makes nearest-neighbour retrieval work well. But when two images are almost the same, and both the penalty and the push blow up. Pathology has many near-duplicate tiles, which is why the pathology variant later in this deck swaps KoLeo for a bounded KDE term.

    KoLeo pushes every class token away from its nearest neighbour, so a batch spreads evenly over the sphere.

    CoCa intuition

    Inside the attentional poolers

    Both poolers are one cross-attention layer with learned queries. They differ only in how many queries they have and where their output goes.

    The attention block

    The generative pooler is one multi-head cross-attention layer, as in a Transformer decoder, but with no residual connection and no MLP. Its queries are learned parameters; its keys and values come from the 256 image tokens.

    The attention block

    The contrastive pooler is the same kind of layer with a single query. Its keys and values are the 256 outputs of the generative pooler. Like the first, it has no residual connection and no MLP.

    Keys and values

    The generative pooler reads the 256 image tokens from the ViT encoder. After a LayerNorm and a linear map, they are the keys and values of a single cross-attention layer.

    Keys and values

    The contrastive pooler sits on top of the generative one: its keys and values are the 256 tokens that the generative pooler produced.

    Learned queries

    The queries are not computed from the image. They are 256 learned vectors, the same for every image, and each one becomes one output token.

    Learned queries

    A single learned query vector, the same for every image. Its job is to summarize the whole image in one embedding.

    Attention weights

    Each query scores every token, and a softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to 1. Different queries learn to look at different parts of the image. The heads of the multi-head layer do this in parallel.

    Attention weights

    The one query scores all 256 tokens. Its weights spread over the whole image, because one vector has to describe all of it.

    Weighted sum

    Each output is the attention-weighted average of the values. Every head does this with its own projections; the heads are concatenated and mixed by . queries always give outputs, whatever the number of image tokens.

    Where it goes

    The 256 outputs are the image side of the multimodal text decoder: every text position cross-attends to them. Their training signal is the captioning loss.

    Where it goes

    The single output, ℓ2-normalized, is the image embedding. The contrastive loss matches it with the text [CLS] embedding, as in CLIP.

    An attentional pooler turns any number of image tokens into n learned summaries: 256 for captioning, 1 for contrastive matching.

    SimCLR intuition

    Understanding NT-Xent

    NT-Xent turns every view into a classification problem: among all the other views in the batch, pick the other view of the same image.

    Two views per image

    A batch of images gives augmented views. Each view goes through the encoder and the projection head and is ℓ2-normalized to a point on the unit sphere. Here .

    Similarity matrix

    Compare every view with every other view: for unit vectors, the dot product is the cosine similarity. The diagonal compares a view with itself and is left out.

    One anchor

    Take one row: anchor . Its positive is the other view of the same image; the remaining views are negatives. Every view takes a turn as the anchor.

    Softmax with temperature

    Divide the row by and apply a softmax, anchor excluded. The loss wants the positive to win. A small sharpens the softmax, so the hardest negatives dominate. Drag the slider.

    Negative log

    The pair loss is minus the log of the positive’s probability: near 0 when the positive takes almost all of it, large when a negative wins.

    Average and train

    Average over all anchors, both orderings of every pair. Training pulls each positive pair together and pushes views of different images apart, and the loss falls.

    0.100.1 in the paper. Lower is sharper.

    NT-Xent is a softmax classification per view: find your own pair among all 2N − 1 candidates.

    I-JEPA intuition

    How the predictor is asked about a target block

    The predictor never sees the target patches. It gets the context tokens plus one query per target patch: the same mask token, tagged with that patch’s position.

    Context tokens

    The context encoder’s outputs are projected to the narrower predictor width and given the positional embeddings of their own patches. These tokens carry all the image content the predictor will see.

    Target positions

    Each patch of target block has a known row and column. Its positional embedding is a fixed 2D sine–cosine code of that location, the same table the encoders use.

    Shared mask token

    One learned vector is copied once per target patch. All copies are identical, so on its own a copy says nothing about which patch it stands for.

    Queries

    Adding the position to each copy gives one query per target patch. The queries differ only in where they point; none of them contains image content.

    Predictor

    The queries are appended to the context tokens and the narrow ViT runs self-attention over the whole sequence. Only the outputs at the query slots are kept and mapped back to the encoder width as the prediction.

    Every target block

    The same mask token is reused for each of the blocks with that block’s positions. Each prediction is compared with the target encoder’s output at those patches, and the L2 errors are averaged.

    Position tells the predictor where to look; the context tells it what is there.

    DINOv2 intuition

    Sinkhorn-Knopp and the Birkhoff polytope

    Sinkhorn-Knopp balances the teacher’s assignments: every image gets a distribution over prototypes, and every prototype gets the same share of the batch.

    Teacher scores

    For a batch of images and prototypes, the teacher’s scores, divided by the temperature and exponentiated, give a positive matrix. Here . One prototype takes most of the mass; left alone, every image would get the same target and training would collapse.

    Normalize columns

    Divide each column by its sum. Every prototype now receives the same total mass, but the rows no longer sum to 1.

    Normalize rows

    Divide each row by its sum, so each image again has a distribution over prototypes. The column sums drift, but less than before.

    Repeat

    Alternating the two steps converges to a matrix whose rows and columns all sum to 1. Only the scaling vectors and change. DINOv2 stops after 3 iterations: about 1% off, close enough for a training target.

    Birkhoff polytope

    The matrices with nonnegative entries and all row and column sums equal to 1 form the Birkhoff polytope. Its vertices are the permutation matrices. For it has 6 vertices and lives in 4 dimensions, so the view is a 3D projection. Every pair of vertices is joined by an edge.

    Birkhoff–von Neumann

    Every doubly stochastic matrix is a convex combination of permutation matrices. The balanced is a mix of several, so each image gets a soft target and every prototype is used equally. With , as in DINOv2, the same idea holds on a transportation polytope; the rows are rescaled to sum to 1 to give each image’s target.

    Sinkhorn-Knopp projects the teacher’s scores onto the doubly stochastic matrices: balanced targets, no collapse.

    BEiT intuition

    The DALL-E dVAE tokenizer

    A discrete variational autoencoder learns a codebook of 8,192 visual words. BEiT borrows its encoder to label every patch with one of them.

    Encode to logits

    The encoder is a convolutional network that downsamples by 8: a 256 px image becomes a grid, a 112 px image a grid. At every cell it outputs 8,192 logits , a categorical distribution over the codebook.

    Gumbel-softmax

    Picking one code is not differentiable. During training the dVAE adds Gumbel noise to the logits and takes a softmax at temperature , giving a soft sample . As is annealed toward 0, the sample approaches one-hot.

    Look up and decode

    The relaxed sample mixes the codebook vectors into one embedding per cell. The decoder upsamples by 8 back to pixels. Coarse color and layout survive; fine texture is lost.

    Training objective

    Encoder, codebook and decoder are trained together, on images alone, to maximize the evidence lower bound: reconstruct the pixels while keeping each close to a uniform prior over the 8,192 codes. DALL-E raised the KL weight to for better codebook usage.

    BEiT’s tokenizer

    BEiT reuses DALL-E’s released dVAE and keeps it frozen. Each 224 px image is resized to 112 px for the tokenizer, so its grid lines up with the ViT’s 16 × 16 px patches. The argmax at each cell is the visual token ; there is no noise, and the decoder is never used.

    2.00Training anneals it toward 0. Lower is closer to one-hot.

    The dVAE gives every 8 × 8 px block of the 112 px view one of 8,192 codes; BEiT freezes it and predicts those codes for masked patches.

    DINOv2 for pathology intuition

    KoLeo vs KDE: why swap the regularizer?

    Both push embeddings apart so tiles don’t collapse to one point. They differ when two embeddings are almost identical.

    KoLeoKDE kernel
    penalty = 0.69 = 4.38
    gradient = −2 = −2.5
    as explodesstays finite, gradient → 0

    von Mises–Fisher (vMF) kernel

    What is vMF?＋
    5
    0 · uniform directions20 · tight concentration

    Dots are vMF samples on a 3D unit sphere, darker near the mean; the ring holds 90% of them. Drag to rotate, double-click to reset. The arrow marks the preferred direction μ.

    View reference image

    von Mises–Fisher (vMF) naturally models directions on a hypersphere.

    zi⊤zj=cos(θij)

    For normalized embeddings, the dot product measures angular similarity. It depends on the angle between their directions, with each embedding having unit magnitude.

    The von Mises–Fisher distribution describes directions on the unit sphere. A preferred direction sets the center of concentration, and κ controls how tightly points cluster around it.

    For normalized embeddings, the vMF kernel gives higher weight to directions with greater cosine similarity. Increasing κ makes this preference sharper.

    k(zi,zj)=eκzi⊤zj
    zi,zj
    Two normalized image embeddings.
    zi⊤zj
    Cosine similarity.
    κ=5
    Controls how sharply the kernel responds to similarity.

    For unit-normalized embeddings, d2=2−2zi⊤zj. Substituting gives

    k(d)=eκe−κd2/2

    A smooth Gaussian-shaped distance profile, highest at zero and decreasing over 0≤d≤2.

    KDE aggregates the entire batch

    LKDE=1N ∑ilog( ∑j≠i eκzi⊤zj)

    For each embedding, sum the kernel similarities to every other embedding in the batch. Take the logarithm, then average over the N anchors.

    Minimize this loss to discourage excessive concentration of embeddings. It is the negative of the paper’s kernel entropy estimator.

    The distance plot shows one pair’s kernel contribution. The batch loss applies a log to the sum of all contributions for each anchor.

    Why a diversity term at all?

    Invariance: two views of the same tile should match, .

    Diversity: different tiles should not all collapse, . DINO’s own tricks help too; this term adds to them.

    KoLeo’s problem in pathology

    Tissue repeats across patients: two normal liver tiles can look almost the same, so often. The push then explodes and can split tiles that should stay close.

    KDE’s fix: a bounded kernel

    The penalty never exceeds , and its gradient fades to 0 near duplicates. Same goal, stable gradients.

    KoLeo’s push explodes for near-duplicate tiles. KDE’s push stays finite.

    Why use a projection head?

    The MLP separates learning useful features from optimizing the contrastive loss.

    Image x→Encoder f→h→MLP g→z→Contrastive loss

    Representation space h

    The encoder produces a rich representation of morphology, texture, color, and other image features.

    These features can support a range of downstream tasks, including tasks that use information affected by the training augmentations.

    Contrastive space z

    The projection head transforms h into z, where the contrastive loss is applied.

    The loss encourages agreement between augmented views. This can suppress augmentation-specific information, such as stain variations.

    A buffer between the objectives

    Applying the loss to z gives the projector room to specialize in augmentation invariance, while h can preserve additional information useful downstream.

    Gradients still flow through the projector to train the encoder.

    After pretraining

    SimCLR found that representations before the projection head, h, performed better on downstream evaluation. Discard the projector and retain the encoder for downstream use.

    DINO intuition

    Why centering and sharpening?

    With no labels, the student can match the teacher trivially by giving every image the same answer. Each operation blocks one way of collapsing.

    Collapse: every output is flatCollapse: one dimension wins for every patchHealthy: confident and different per patch

    Patch 1
    Patch 2
    Patch 3
    avgBatch average

    teacher output over dimensions = 1 … 8

    Centering: subtract a running mean

    is the average teacher output over recent batches. Subtracting it means no single dimension can win for every image.

    On its own, centering pushes the teacher toward a flat, uniform output. A flat target tells the student nothing.

    Sharpening: a lower teacher temperature

    Dividing by a small makes the teacher’s softmax peaked and confident, sharper than the student’s ().

    On its own, sharpening lets one dimension win for every image, so every image looks the same.

    Together: confident and diverse

    Centering keeps the dimensions balanced across the batch. Sharpening keeps each image’s target confident.

    The two pull in opposite directions, so the teacher can’t settle into either collapse.

    Each patch gets its own clear target, so the student has something real to learn.

    Centering stops one dimension from dominating. Sharpening stops the output from going flat. You need both.
